analysis.one_liner: Lets banks, securities firms, and insurers combine into single financial companies, repealing the Glass-Steagall separation.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees, sent to a subcommittee in March 1999, and never received a House vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would repeal the Glass-Steagall rules that kept banks separate from securities firms and insurance companies, letting a single holding company run a bank, a securities broker, and an insurer under one roof. It would let bank holding companies engage in any activity the Federal Reserve and Treasury jointly decide is 'financial in nature,' including merchant banking — owning stakes in nonfinancial companies. It includes a consumer title requiring disclosure that investment products sold at banks are not FDIC-insured, and it blocks many state laws from restricting these new combinations.
analysis.who_benefits: Large bank holding companies, securities firms, and insurance companies gain the ability to merge into diversified financial conglomerates, enter each other's businesses, cross-market products, and hold equity stakes in nonfinancial companies through merchant banking provisions. Consumers get one-stop financial shopping and some new disclosure and suitability rules for products sold at bank branches.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Glass-Steagall provisions barring affiliations between Federal Reserve member banks and securities firms, and repeals the ban on interlocking directors between banks and securities firms.

Lets bank holding companies engage in any activity the Federal Reserve and Treasury jointly determine to be financial in nature or incidental to it, including insurance, securities underwriting, and financial advisory work.
Authorizes merchant banking: a bank holding company may acquire and hold ownership stakes in companies engaged in otherwise impermissible activities, holding them for later resale.

Requires that a holding company's banks be well capitalized, well managed, and rated satisfactory or better under the Community Reinvestment Act before it can use the new powers — a condition tying expansion to community lending records.

Title IV directs federal banking agencies to write customer protection rules for nondeposit products sold by banks, including anti-coercion rules, suitability standards, disclosure that products are not FDIC-insured, and physical separation of banking and investment sales.

analysis.who_pays: The safety net behind insured deposits would extend, at least in structure, to conglomerates combining banking with riskier securities and insurance activities. Consumers would face cross-marketing of uninsured, unregulated-elsewhere investment products through their bank relationship. State regulators lose authority over many affiliations and sales practices, and smaller financial firms would compete against giants combining banking, securities, and insurance under one roof.
analysis.who_pays_short: Depositors, bank customers, and small financial firms

drawbacks.text: Repealing the Glass-Steagall affiliation barriers ties banks holding federally insured deposits to securities and insurance activities, so losses in a securities or insurance affiliate could pressure the insured bank and, ultimately, the federal deposit insurance fund.

The bill preempts state laws that restrict affiliations among banks, insurers, and national banks, and bars states from regulating bank insurance activities in ways that treat banks less favorably than other insurers — shrinking state-level consumer protections.

Sections 111 and 10A sharply limit the Federal Reserve's authority to examine, impose capital rules on, or take action against nonbank subsidiaries of holding companies, leaving each subsidiary supervised by its own 'functional' regulator and no regulator watching the whole conglomerate.

The key operative standard — what counts as 'financial in nature' — is left to a joint determination by the Federal Reserve and Treasury, a broad delegation that the industry could later expand through regulation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill pairs a sweeping structural change — erasing the legal wall between banking, securities, and insurance — with genuine consumer provisions: CRA conditions, firewalls between banks and their subsidiaries, disclosure rules for uninsured products, and anti-coercion standards. The consumer protections, however, sit downstream of the main event: the bill's engine is consolidation, and its approach to risk is to trust functional regulation, where each piece of a conglomerate is supervised separately and the Federal Reserve is largely locked out of the nonbank pieces. An honest supporter could defend the convenience and efficiency arguments; an honest critic would point to concentration and the dilution of oversight over combined firms, costs that would fall on depositors and customers rather than shareholders.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Banking and Commerce committees and then in a Commerce subcommittee, never got a committee report or floor vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. John LaFalce of New York introduced the bill on February 10, 1999, joined by original cosponsors Reps. Vento, Baker, Capuano, and Ackerman; it drew six cosponsors in total, four Democrats and two Republicans.
The bill was referred the same day to the Committee on Banking and Financial Services and, in addition, to the Committee on Commerce.
On March 1, 1999, the House referred it to the Commerce Committee's Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials; no further action followed.
The bill never advanced past the committee stage — no markup, no report, no floor vote — and expired when the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the legal separation of banking, securities, and insurance technically lasted a few months longer, which spared state regulators and consumer protections in this version. But that is cold comfort: the same basic repeal — allowing bank-securities-insurance conglomerates — became law in November 1999 through the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, so large financial institutions got what this bill would have given them regardless, through a different vehicle.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo briefly; conglomerates later won anyway

for.name: Rep. John J. LaFalce
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, which he framed as a prudential framework for bank-securities-insurance affiliation with consumer protections attached.

for.name: Reps. Vento, Capuano, Ackerman (D) and Baker (R)
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors when the bill was introduced; the bill drew six cosponsors overall, four Democrats and two Republicans.

against.name: House Committee on Banking and Financial Services
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never reported it out; no markup or committee vote is recorded.

against.name: House Commerce Subcommittee on Finance and Hazardous Materials
against.what_they_did: Received a referral of the bill on March 1, 1999 and took no recorded action on it.

sides.party_line_note: The bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call record exists; its sponsorship was bipartisan, with a Democratic lead sponsor and cosponsors split four Democrats to two Republicans.

industries.industry: Large banks and bank holding companies
industries.note: The bill would let them become full-service financial conglomerates — banking plus securities plus insurance plus merchant banking stakes — while using the goodwill and deposit base of insured banks. Customers gain convenience, but the deposit safety net and cross-selling pressure extend to riskier activities.

The repeal of Glass-Steagall's affiliation bans opens the door for securities firms to combine with, or be acquired by, banks, and for banks to underwrite securities — expanding the market and consolidating it in the process.

Insurers could become financial holding companies and acquire banks, but the bill simultaneously bars national banks from underwriting title insurance and most insurance as principal, and preserves the McCarran-Ferguson Act and state licensing — so it opens some doors and closes others.

industries.industry: Community banks and small financial firms
industries.note: The new powers flow to holding companies that can meet well-capitalized, well-managed thresholds, favoring the largest institutions; smaller banks and firms would compete against conglomerates that can cross-market and cross-subsidize. Their competitive concern overlaps with public worries about financial concentration.
